e.t: This word means “silver,” referring either to the metal itself or to silver used as money. It is a noun that can identify a monetary amount or possession rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 20 times, including passages involving entrusted money and Judas’s payment. The basic meaning remains the material or monetary value of silver; the surrounding sentence determines whether the emphasis is on coins, wealth, or the metal. Its first occurrence is in Matthew 25:18 and its last in 1 Peter 1:18.

It can describe a spoken denial, such as refusing to admit knowing someone, and it can also express rejecting or turning away from a claim or allegiance. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 33 times, showing a repeated concern with whether people acknowledge or reject a relationship or commitment. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: This word refers to the person responsible for overseeing a banquet—the head waiter or master of the banquet. It describes an official serving role at a feast, not simply an ordinary guest or servant. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all within two verses in John 2:8–9. The word’s basic meaning identifies someone who managed or supervised the banquet service. Its precise role in those verses depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to the person in charge of the feast’s arrangements.

e.t: The word means “opportunity.” It refers to a favorable occasion or opening that can be used for some purpose. As a noun, it identifies the occasion itself rather than the action taken in response to it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times across six verses, including passages in Romans, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, and 1 Timothy. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This word means “to live,” describing the act or condition of being alive. It functions as a verb, pointing to living rather than merely existing as an idea or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Peter 4:2. Its basic meaning is clear from its direct gloss and translation as “live”; the surrounding verse determines the particular force of that living in context.

e.t: This word means “food,” referring to what a person eats for nourishment. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Timothy 6:8, and its basic sense is plainly material provision rather than an abstract idea. The word belongs to the ordinary language of daily bodily needs, alongside other necessities of life. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the word itself directly identifies food as something needed for living. This Greek New Testament word is distinct from similarly rendered words in other biblical corpora.

e.t: This word refers to “dissension” or “division”—a state of disagreement that separates people rather than uniting them. It describes discord as a recognizable condition within a community or group. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Romans 16:17 and Galatians 5:20. Those references identify its limited distribution, while the central sense remains the presence of serious disagreement or splitting among people. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage and the actions or attitudes being discussed.

The idea includes steady restraint, thoughtful conduct, and personal discipline. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Titus 1:8, so its normal meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. Its English rendering is “self-controlled,” which closely expresses the same central idea.

It identifies a person by belonging to the nations rather than to Israel’s covenant community. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, all in four verses: three in Matthew and once in 3 John. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: This word means “be enraged,” describing a person who is intensely angry or furious. It functions as a verb, expressing a strong emotional reaction rather than a calm disagreement or mild irritation. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, so its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context. The word’s basic sense remains clear: to become or be fiercely angry. Its single occurrence is recorded in Acts 26:11.

The word’s basic meaning remains “to rebuke”; the surrounding verse determines the specific manner and reason for that correction.

The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 11:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is being thoroughly outfitted for a task or conflict.

In the Greek New Testament, it occurs nine times, chiefly in Hebrews, where it is repeatedly associated with entering or failing to enter God’s rest. Its use in Acts also refers to rest in relation to God’s dwelling. The central idea remains a condition of rest rather than ongoing labor or disturbance.

In the Greek New Testament, it appears three times, each time carrying the idea of remembrance. Its meaning points readers toward preserving the memory of someone or something so that it remains before others. The surrounding verse determines what is being remembered and why that remembrance matters.

It is used once in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew 23:37. The word’s central picture is a small, dependent young bird, a meaning that can naturally support an image of care and protection when the surrounding passage provides that context. Its precise force in Matthew depends on the verse and its surrounding words.

It is a descriptive term for terrain, so its basic meaning concerns the shape and elevation of the land. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs two times, both in Luke, showing a limited and specific use within that corpus. The word itself identifies the landscape without, by itself, explaining anything about the people or events associated with it.

This word means “to do one’s best” or “to supplement,” expressing the effort to add something needed or to contribute fully. It describes active involvement rather than passive receiving. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Peter 1:5. The broader sense is to bring forward an additional contribution or make every effort toward what is required. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and context, which are handled separately from this word’s basic lexical meaning.

It describes something exceeding what is ordinary or already present, and it normally strengthens the action or quality being discussed rather than naming a person or thing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 12 times in 11 verses, with most occurrences in 2 Corinthians. Its exact force depends on what it modifies in each sentence, but its central idea is clear: something is greater, fuller, or beyond measure.

Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the misuse of another person’s trust, circumstances, or rights for one’s own gain.

Its exact force depends on what is being questioned in the sentence. It occurs 27 times in 27 New Testament verses, including questions in Matthew, Mark, Luke, Romans, and Hebrews.

The surrounding passage is needed to explain what happened there, but the word itself refers to Samos.
